analysis.one_liner: Bans federal facial recognition and biometric surveillance unless Congress specifically authorizes it.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in March 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for any federal agency, employee, or contractor to acquire or use facial recognition or other remote biometric surveillance—like face, gait, or voice identification—unless Congress passes a law specifically authorizing that use with accuracy and privacy safeguards attached. It would also cut off federal Byrne public-safety grants to state and local governments that use biometric surveillance without a substantially similar ban, and it would let individuals and state attorneys general sue over violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who would otherwise be scanned without their knowledge: pedestrians, travelers at airports and border zones, drivers, and people attending protests or houses of worship. People wrongly identified by facial recognition—which has documented higher error rates for women and people with darker skin—would also gain a right to sue for damages.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any federal agency, official, contractor, or subcontractor from acquiring, possessing, or using facial recognition or other remote biometric surveillance in the United States, including airports, ports of entry, and border zones, unless an act of Congress specifically authorizes it with accuracy standards, audit trails, and due-process protections.

Makes information obtained through illegal biometric surveillance inadmissible in any federal proceeding, and gives aggrieved individuals the right to sue for actual and punitive damages plus attorneys' fees, with state attorneys general also able to sue on residents' behalf.

Withholds federal Byrne public-safety grant money from state and local governments that do not adopt a substantially similar ban, and prohibits federal law enforcement funds from being spent on biometric surveillance systems.
Allows NIST to keep testing and researching the technology, and does not preempt stricter state or local laws, so existing stronger protections remain intact.

analysis.who_pays: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance companies lose the government market: federal agencies could not buy or use their systems, and state and local police would have to give up the technology or lose Byrne grant funding. Law enforcement agencies also lose an investigative tool.
analysis.who_pays_short: Biometric tech vendors and police agencies

drawbacks.text: A flat ban removes facial recognition even for uses many people support, such as identifying crime suspects or finding missing persons; law enforcement groups generally argue the technology is a legitimate investigative tool when properly regulated.

The only path to future use is a congressional act that meets very detailed requirements—naming the entity, the technology, accuracy rates by gender and skin color, and audit mechanisms—a high bar some would call an impractical substitute for routine regulation.
Governments that keep using the technology would forfeit Byrne grant funding, reducing money available for other public-safety priorities in those jurisdictions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gain is real and direct: the bill targets government face-scanning of people who never consented, in a technology with documented accuracy problems that fall hardest on women and people of color. The cost is that police lose an investigative tool, though the bill preserves NIST testing and leaves a specific legislative path for authorized uses. The design leans toward prohibition rather than regulation, which is the main good-faith objection.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees after referral and died when the 118th Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act of 2023 on March 7, 2023, with 14 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Oversight and Accountability Committee, and the record shows no further action—no hearing, markup, or floor vote—before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill would have prohibited federal agencies and officials from using facial recognition and other remote biometric surveillance without an explicit act of Congress, and would have conditioned federal Byrne law enforcement grants on state and local governments adopting similar bans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance vendors keep selling to federal, state, and local governments, and law enforcement agencies keep using the technology without the restrictions or private right of action this bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Biometric surveillance vendors and police agencies

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance software vendors
industries.note: The bill cuts off their government market: federal agencies and contractors could not buy or use their systems, and state and local police would have to abandon the technology to keep Byrne grant funding. These companies profit from selling identification of people who never consented, so their interest runs against the privacy of ordinary people.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Police would lose a surveillance and investigative tool and, at the state and local level, risk Byrne grant funds for continuing to use it. Some agencies argue the tool helps solve crimes; civil-rights groups and people misidentified by the technology argue it harms the public.
